subject: AI & Agents
title: Classification: Sorting Into Buckets
description: One-minute skill: Classification: Sorting Into Buckets.

hook.text: Is this email spam or not? Is this mole cancerous or benign? That's classification.

buildup.text: Classification assigns inputs to predefined categories based on learned patterns.

discovery.text: The model draws decision boundaries — lines (or curves) that separate one class from another.

twist.text: Real-world categories overlap. A borderline case might be 51% spam. What do you do?

climax.text: Classification powers fraud detection, medical diagnosis, content moderation, and more.

punchline.text: Life is messy. Classification draws clean lines through the mess.

quiz.question: What does a classification model do?

details.summary: Classification assigns inputs to predefined categories — sorting emails into spam or not spam, identifying diseases from scans, or detecting objects in images. It is one of ML's most fundamental tasks.
details.whyItMatters: Classification powers countless everyday AI applications. Understanding how it works reveals why false positives and false negatives occur and how to tune the tradeoff between them.
takeaways: Classification assigns inputs to discrete predefined categories
It powers spam filters, medical diagnosis, and content moderation
False positives and false negatives require careful tradeoff tuning

faq.question: How does a classification model make its decision?
faq.answer: The model computes probability scores for each possible category. Inputs are assigned to the category with the highest score. A threshold can be adjusted to favor precision or recall depending on the application.

faq.question: Why is classification sometimes wrong?
faq.answer: Edge cases between categories, examples unlike anything in training, and noisy data all cause errors. No classifier achieves perfect accuracy on real-world data because the world contains inherent ambiguity.
